query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Depositing a high‐entropy alloy (HEA) coating onto a copper matrix will improve the wear resistance and surface protection of the copper, compared to an uncoated substrate.
generation.material_initial_state: A copper (Cu) matrix, which has excellent thermal and electrical properties but relatively low wear resistance and poor surface oxidation protection.
generation.intervention: Apply a thin, adherent coating of a high‐entropy alloy – for example, a refractory or eutectic HEA such as an AlCoCrFeNi (or a similar variant that forms a stable solid solution with protective oxides) – onto the Cu substrate using an appropriate deposition method (e.g., laser cladding, sputtering, or other additive manufacturing technique).
generation.conditions: The coated composite is evaluated under room‐temperature and elevated‐temperature wear conditions, as well as under cyclic thermal exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The HEA coating, with its multiprincipal element solid solution (either FCC, BCC, or a dual-phase microstructure), will develop a hard, wear‐resistant layer. In addition, upon exposure (especially at high temperatures), the formation of protective oxide species (e.g., Al2O3 or Cr2O3) at the surface further mediates adhesion and protection.
generation.mechanism: The HEA layer acts as a mechanical barrier that reduces material removal by abrasion via its high hardness and complex microstructural features (such as lattice distortion and sluggish diffusion). Moreover, the intrinsic oxidation resistance of the HEA leads to the formation of a self-healing oxide film that further protects the underlying Cu matrix from corrosive and high‐temperature environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: The copper composite coated with the HEA is predicted to show a significantly reduced wear rate and enhanced surface oxidation resistance relative to the uncoated Cu substrate, thereby extending its service life in friction-intensive or high-temperature applications.
generation.baseline: A bare Cu matrix, which exhibits high wear and oxidation degradation under demanding conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the HEA coating will depend on the quality of adhesion (influenced by deposition parameters and interfacial bonding) and on thermal expansion mismatch between Cu and the HEA; extreme thermal cycles or mechanical stresses beyond moderate levels could lead to delamination or microcracking.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative improvement in wear and oxidation resistance is expected based on known HEA properties, the precise magnitude of the improvement and the optimal HEA composition for best adhesion to Cu remain uncertain without targeted experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: (1) Cu substrates coated with the selected HEA using the same deposition method and (2) uncoated Cu substrates. Subject both sets to identical wear tests (e.g., pin-on-disk abrasion) and high-temperature oxidation tests in a controlled atmosphere. Characterize damage (wear track depth, mass loss, and oxide formation) after defined cycling.
measurements: Mass change during oxidation (mg/cm2) via thermogravimetric analysis
Adhesion strength of the HEA coating via scratch testing
Microstructural analysis (SEM/EDS, XRD) of the coating and interface after testing
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the HEA-coated Cu samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in wear resistance (i.e., lower wear rate and mass gain) and maintain coating integrity compared to the uncoated Cu specimens under identical testing conditions, or if the coating fails to adhere properly (e.g., delamination occurs under moderate stress), then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs), since their discovery by Yeh et al. in 2004, [1] have opened up researchers to a new alloy system that contains five or more equimolar principal elements. In equimolar HEAs, each element has an equal probability of occupying the lattice sites in a crystal structure such as face-centered cubic (FCC), [2] body-centered cubic (BCC), [3] or hexagonal structure [4] crystal structures. Lattice distortion, sluggish diffusion, high entropy, and cocktail effects have been identified as the core effects contributing to the superior properties, hardness, strength, ductility, erosion, tribocorrosion, corrosion, and oxidation/wear resistance [5] − [7] of HEAs in a wide range of temperatures over conventional alloys. From the viewpoint of applications in extrusion dies and cutting inserts, the cost of metal powders used to develop bulk HEAs can hinder their commercialization as an alternative to the alloys in use. Abstract A novel metal matrix composite based on the NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy (HEA) was designed by the in-situ formation method. The microstructure, phase evolution, and compression mechanical properties at room temperature of the composite are investigated in detail. The results confirmed that the composite was primarily composed of body-centered cubic solid solution with a small amount of titanium carbides and alumina. With the presence of approximately 7.0 vol. % Al 2 O 3 and 32.2 vol. % TiC reinforced particles, the compressive fracture strength of the composite (1542 MPa) was increased by approximately 50% compared with that of the as-cast NbMoCrTiAl HEA. In consideration of the superior oxidation resistance, the P/M NbMoCrTiAl high entropy alloy composite could be considered as a promising high temperature structural material. Keywords: high entropy alloys, metal matrix composites, mechanical properties
